sections.title: The Real Reason Teams Split — And Why Most Shouldn't Yet
sections.content:
Every conference talk makes microservices sound like the obvious evolution from monoliths. The reality is messier. **Netflix, Amazon, and Uber migrated because their monoliths couldn't keep up** — not with traffic, but with organizational velocity. When 200 engineers commit to the same codebase, merge conflicts become the bottleneck, not CPU.

The decision to split is fundamentally an organizational one, not a technical one. Conway's Law tells us that systems mirror communication structures — if you have three independent teams that rarely need to coordinate, microservices let each team own, deploy, and scale their slice without waiting for the other two. But if your team is 8 people working on a single product, microservices introduce network calls, distributed debugging, and operational overhead for no organizational payoff.

The trap most teams fall into is splitting too early, before the domain boundaries are clear. You end up with services that constantly call each other for every operation — a **distributed monolith** that has all the latency of network calls plus all the coupling of shared code. Amazon's famous "two-pizza team" rule wasn't about architecture — it was about team autonomy. The service boundaries followed the team boundaries, not the other way around.

Measure before splitting. If your deployment lead time is under a day, your teams rarely block each other's releases, and your monolith handles current load, the honest answer is: don't split yet. The strongest signal to split is **deploy contention** — track how often teams block each other's releases and how often a change in module A breaks module B. Those metrics tell you where the real seams are.

sections.title: What You Actually Gain and Lose
sections.content:
| Dimension | Monolith | Microservices |
|---|---|---|
| Deployment | Single artifact, one CI pipeline | Per-service CI/CD — multiply pipelines by service count |
| Scalability | Scale everything together (wasteful if one module is hot) | Scale only the hot service — inventory scales independently from auth |
| Team autonomy | Shared codebase, shared release train | Independent ownership, independent deploys |
| Latency | In-process method calls (~nanoseconds) | Network round trips (~1-10ms per hop) |
| Transactions | Single ACID database — rollback is trivial | Sagas with compensating transactions — rollback is code you write |
| Debugging | Stack trace from top to bottom | Distributed tracing required — one request spans 5 log files |
| Data model | Shared schema, easy JOINs | Database-per-service, no cross-service JOINs |
| Operational cost | One app to monitor, deploy, and page about | N services × (CI/CD + monitoring + alerts + on-call rotation) |

sections.title: The Decision Framework: Concrete Signals, Not Vibes
sections.content:
**Stay monolith when** your team is under 15 engineers, the domain is not well-understood (startup finding product-market fit), you lack DevOps maturity for running distributed systems, or your current deploy frequency is acceptable. A well-structured monolith with clean module boundaries gives you 80% of the organizational benefit with 20% of the operational cost.

**Split when** any of these are true: teams routinely block each other's deployments (measure mean time between merge and production — if it exceeds 3 days due to coordination, that's a signal), one module needs 10× the compute of others (a search index shouldn't force you to scale the auth module), regulatory compliance requires data isolation (PCI for payments, HIPAA for health records), or you have well-understood bounded contexts confirmed by at least 6 months of stable domain modeling.

**The two-pizza team rule** is the organizational heuristic: if a service can't be owned by a team of 6-10 people who can be fed by two pizzas, the service boundary is wrong. Services should map to team ownership — one team owns one service, one service has one team. Shared ownership of a service recreates the merge-conflict problem microservices were supposed to solve.

For migration, the **Strangler Fig pattern** is the only safe approach at scale. Route traffic at the API gateway to new services incrementally — start with low-risk, well-bounded domains (user profiles, notifications) before touching revenue-critical flows (checkout, payments). The monolith keeps serving everything the new services haven't replaced. Never attempt a big-bang rewrite — the failure rate of "rewrite from scratch" projects in production systems is historically above 70%.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Deploy contention is the strongest split signal** — teams blocking each other's releases; merge-to-production >3 days indicates the right seam.
- **Two-pizza team = service boundary** — 6–10 people own one service end-to-end; shared ownership recreates coordination problems.
- **Distributed monolith trap** — splitting code without splitting data gives you network latency plus tight coupling; no real independence.
- **Operational tax is multiplicative** — each service adds CI/CD, monitoring, alerts, and on-call rotation; budget 3–5 hours per service per week.
- **Strangler Fig over big-bang rewrite** — route traffic incrementally at the gateway; big-bang rewrites fail >70% of the time.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Microservices give you independent deployability and independent scalability — but at the cost of in-process calls, shared-database transactions, and simple single-service debugging. The decision should not be about the pattern's popularity but about whether you have a concrete problem that microservices solve better than a well-structured monolith.

**When the split makes sense:**
- Deploy contention is the clearest signal — when teams routinely block each other's releases and merge-to-production takes three days due to coordination overhead, that organizational friction is exactly what microservices fix
- Scaling skew is the second signal — when one module needs 10× the compute of everything else, you're paying to scale the whole monolith to support one hot component
- Domain boundaries should be stable for at least six months before extracting — use Domain-Driven Design to identify bounded contexts first

**The distributed monolith trap:**
- Splitting code without splitting data or decoupling call paths gives you network latency plus tight coupling — no real independence gained
- If Service A can't deploy without coordinating with Service B, you haven't actually split; you've just added network hops to your monolith
- Services that call each other synchronously for every operation recreate the coordination problem in a more expensive form

**How to migrate safely:**
- Always use the Strangler Fig pattern — route traffic at the gateway incrementally to new services while the monolith handles everything else
- Start with low-risk, well-bounded domains like notifications or user profiles, not payments or checkout
- Maintain a rollback path at every step — gateway routing is a one-line revert, and the monolith's code stays intact for at least one release cycle

I recommend the monolith-first default: only split when you can name the concrete problem — deploy contention, scaling skew, or team ownership — that microservices solve better than a modular monolith.

questions.question: What is an API Gateway and how do you implement one with Spring Cloud Gateway?
questions.title: API Gateway with Spring Cloud Gateway
questions.direct_answer: An API Gateway is a single entry point that handles cross-cutting concerns (routing, auth, rate limiting, SSL termination) across all microservices. Spring Cloud Gateway uses reactive WebFlux and replaces the deprecated Netflix Zuul.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the gateway's role as a cross-cutting-concern handler
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Implementing business logic in the gateway — it should be a thin routing layer
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Circuit Breaker filter and the risk of the gateway becoming a single point of failure

sections.title: Why Every Microservices Architecture Needs a Front Door
sections.content:
Without an API gateway, a mobile app calling your microservices needs to know the addresses of every service — orders at `10.0.1.5:8080`, users at `10.0.2.3:8081`, payments at `10.0.3.7:8082`. Every time you add, remove, or scale a service, every client needs updating. That's the **N-endpoint problem**, and it gets worse fast.

The API gateway is a reverse proxy that sits between clients and your service fleet. Clients call one URL. The gateway routes each request to the right backend based on the path, applies cross-cutting concerns — authentication, rate limiting, SSL termination, request logging — and returns the response. This centralizes concerns that would otherwise be duplicated in every service: token validation, CORS headers, request throttling.

**Spring Cloud Gateway** replaced Netflix Zuul as the Spring ecosystem's gateway. The architectural difference matters: Zuul 1 was servlet-based (one thread per request), which meant 200 concurrent connections needed 200 threads. Spring Cloud Gateway is built on **Project Reactor and Netty** — it's fully non-blocking. A single thread can handle thousands of concurrent connections because it never blocks waiting for a downstream response. For a gateway that terminates all external traffic, this concurrency model is the right choice.

The critical design principle: keep the gateway **thin**. Authentication, rate limiting, circuit breaking, and routing belong here. Business logic does not. A gateway that calls multiple downstream services, aggregates responses, and applies business rules becomes a bottleneck monolith at the edge. For response aggregation, use the BFF (Backend-for-Frontend) pattern with dedicated composition services behind the gateway.

sections.title: Route Configuration — How Requests Find Their Service
sections.content:
Spring Cloud Gateway routes are defined by three things: a **predicate** (which requests match), a **URI** (where to forward them), and **filters** (what to do in transit). The YAML configuration is the most common approach for straightforward routing.

```yaml
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: order-service
          uri: lb://ORDER-SERVICE          # lb:// = load-balanced via service discovery
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/orders/**
            - Method=GET,POST,PUT
          filters:
            - StripPrefix=1                # removes /api before forwarding
            - AddRequestHeader=X-Gateway-Source, spring-cloud-gateway
        - id: user-service
          uri: lb://USER-SERVICE
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/users/**
          filters:
            - StripPrefix=1
```

The `lb://` prefix is doing real work here — it resolves the logical service name (`ORDER-SERVICE`) through the service registry (Eureka, Consul, or Kubernetes DNS) and load-balances across healthy instances. Without it, you'd hardcode IPs that break every time an instance scales or restarts.

Predicates can match on path, method, headers, query parameters, cookies, or time windows. For programmatic routing — when the logic is more complex than YAML can express — use the fluent Java DSL, which gives you the same capabilities with compile-time safety.

```java
@Bean
public RouteLocator customRoutes(RouteLocatorBuilder builder) {
    return builder.routes()
        .route("order-service", r -> r
            .path("/api/orders/**")
            .and().method(HttpMethod.GET, HttpMethod.POST)
            .filters(f -> f.stripPrefix(1)
                          .addRequestHeader("X-Request-Start",
                              String.valueOf(System.currentTimeMillis())))
            .uri("lb://ORDER-SERVICE"))
        .build();
}
```

Use YAML for simple, static routes. Use Java DSL when routing depends on runtime conditions or when you want refactoring support from the IDE.

sections.title: Cross-Cutting Filters — Auth, Rate Limiting, and Circuit Breaking
The Gateway as a Single Point of Failure — And How to Prevent It
sections.content:
The gateway terminates all external traffic. If it goes down, every service is unreachable — it's the most critical single point of failure in the architecture. Production deployments must address this.

Run **at least three gateway instances** behind a cloud load balancer (AWS ALB, GCP Cloud Load Balancer, or an Nginx ingress controller in Kubernetes). The load balancer health-checks each gateway instance and removes unhealthy ones. In Kubernetes, the deployment looks straightforward.

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-gateway
spec:
  replicas: 3                        # minimum for production
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 1              # at most 1 down during deploys
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: gateway
        image: myregistry/api-gateway:2.1
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
          limits:
            memory: "1Gi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /actuator/health/readiness
            port: 8080
          periodSeconds: 5
```

The readiness probe ensures Kubernetes only routes traffic to gateway instances that have completed startup and registered with the service registry. Without it, requests hit instances that haven't loaded route configurations yet, returning 404s during rolling deployments.

Monitor three gateway metrics: **request rate** (baseline for capacity planning), **error rate by route** (detects backend failures before users notice), and **p99 latency** (catches slow backends before they cascade). Alert when the gateway's own latency — excluding downstream time — exceeds 10ms, because that means the gateway itself is under resource pressure.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`lb://` + service discovery** — logical service names resolve through Eureka/Consul/K8s DNS; hardcoded IPs break on every scale event.
- **Non-blocking reactor model** — Spring Cloud Gateway uses Netty + Project Reactor; Zuul 1's thread-per-request exhausted pools under load.
- **Thin gateway discipline** — auth, rate limiting, and routing belong here; business logic belongs in BFF services behind the gateway.
- **Circuit breaker per route** — one slow backend (30s responses) blocks the event loop and starves healthy routes without it.
- **SPOF mitigation** — run ≥3 instances behind a load balancer; alert when gateway-internal latency exceeds 10ms.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
An API gateway solves the N-endpoint problem — without it, every client needs to know the address of every microservice, handle auth tokens per service, and update when services scale or move. The gateway is a single front door that handles routing, JWT validation, rate limiting, and TLS termination centrally for all downstream services.

**Spring Cloud Gateway internals:**
- Built on Project Reactor and Netty — fully non-blocking, one thread handles thousands of concurrent connections; this is the key difference from old Netflix Zuul's thread-per-request model that exhausted pools under load
- Routes are defined with predicates (path, method, headers) and filters (strip prefix, add headers, rate limit); the `lb://` URI scheme integrates with service discovery so routes use logical service names instead of hardcoded IPs
- A `GlobalFilter` applies to every request — implement JWT validation here so downstream services never see unauthenticated traffic

**The pitfalls:**
- The gateway is a single point of failure — if it crashes, every service is unreachable; run at least three instances behind a load balancer with readiness probes
- Keep the gateway thin — authentication and rate limiting belong here, but business orchestration does not; a gateway that calls five services and merges their responses is a monolith at the edge
- Circuit breaker per route prevents one slow backend from blocking the event loop and starving healthy routes

I recommend Spring Cloud Gateway over Zuul for any new setup, and keeping the gateway strictly thin — cross-cutting concerns only, no business logic.

questions.question: When do you choose REST vs gRPC vs messaging (Kafka) for inter-service communication?
questions.title: REST vs gRPC vs Messaging — Inter-Service Communication
questions.direct_answer: REST for simple synchronous CRUD. gRPC for high-performance internal RPC with strong contracts. Kafka/messaging for async event-driven flows where services must be decoupled.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of synchronous vs asynchronous communication trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defaulting to REST for everything including high-volume internal calls
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention temporal coupling (sync) vs behavioral coupling (async) as the core trade-off

sections.title: The Coupling Axis That Determines Everything
sections.content:
Every inter-service call is a coupling decision. The question isn't "which protocol is best" — it's **what kind of coupling can this interaction tolerate?**

REST and gRPC create **temporal coupling** — Service A blocks until Service B responds. Both services must be running, healthy, and fast at the same moment. If the order service calls the inventory service via REST and inventory is slow (3-second response instead of 200ms), the order service's threads pile up waiting. At 100 concurrent orders, that's 100 threads blocked. Add a third synchronous dependency and you've built a call chain where the slowest link determines everyone's latency.

Messaging (Kafka, RabbitMQ) breaks temporal coupling by introducing a **broker** between services. Service A publishes an event and moves on — it doesn't care if Service B is running, fast, or even exists. The broker durably stores the message until Service B is ready to process it. The trade-off: you lose immediate response and get eventual consistency instead.

The most common failure pattern in production microservices is an **all-synchronous call chain** without proper resilience. Service A calls B calls C calls D — synchronously. D's database runs a slow query, D responds in 5 seconds, C times out at 10 seconds, B times out at 15 seconds, A returns a 504 to the user after 20 seconds. Meanwhile, 200 threads are blocked across four services. Circuit breakers and timeouts mitigate this, but the root cause is synchronous coupling where async would have been appropriate.

sections.title: REST vs gRPC vs Kafka — The Trade-off Matrix
sections.content:
| Dimension | REST (HTTP/JSON) | gRPC (HTTP/2+Protobuf) | Kafka/Messaging |
|---|---|---|---|
| Coupling | Temporal — both must be up | Temporal — both must be up | Decoupled — broker absorbs gaps |
| Latency | 5–50ms per hop (JSON parse + HTTP/1.1) | 1–10ms per hop (binary + multiplexed) | 10–500ms (broker + consumer poll) |
| Throughput ceiling | ~5K–10K req/s per instance | ~20K–50K req/s per instance | Millions of events/sec (partitioned) |
| Payload efficiency | JSON ~500 bytes for typical message | Protobuf ~50–100 bytes (5–10× smaller) | Protobuf/Avro — same as gRPC |
| Schema enforcement | Optional (OpenAPI/Swagger) | Mandatory (.proto contracts) | Registry-enforced (Avro/Protobuf) |
| Streaming | No native support | Bidirectional streaming built-in | Consumer pulls continuously |
| Debugging | Trivial — curl, browser, Postman | Harder — needs grpcurl or Bloom RPC | Harder — kafkacat + distributed tracing |
| Error handling | HTTP status codes, immediate | gRPC status codes, immediate | DLQ + retry policies, delayed |
| Best fit | External APIs, browser/mobile clients | Internal high-RPS service calls | Event fan-out, async side effects |

sections.title: The Decision Tree for Real Systems
sections.content:
**REST when:** the caller needs an immediate response and the communication is with external consumers (browser, mobile app, third-party partner). Every developer knows how to call a REST API. Tooling is universal — curl, Postman, Swagger, browser network tabs. HTTP caching works natively with CDNs. For public APIs, REST is the only serious option because you can't require every consumer to install a protobuf compiler.

**gRPC when:** both sides are internal services you control, call frequency is high (thousands per second), and payload efficiency matters. Protobuf's binary encoding is 5–10× smaller than JSON, and HTTP/2 multiplexing means multiple concurrent RPCs share one TCP connection instead of opening a new one per request. At Uber, the internal service mesh handles millions of gRPC calls per second — the latency savings compound when requests traverse 5+ service hops.

**Kafka/messaging when:** the producer doesn't need a response, multiple consumers react to the same event, or the workload can tolerate eventual consistency. The canonical example: an order is placed, and inventory, notifications, analytics, and fraud detection all need to know. With REST, the order service calls four services sequentially (or manages parallel async calls with error handling). With Kafka, it publishes one `OrderPlaced` event — each consumer processes independently, at its own pace, and adding a fifth consumer requires zero changes to the producer.

Most production architectures use **all three**. REST at the edge for browser/mobile clients. gRPC for internal hot paths where latency matters (payment authorization, real-time pricing). Kafka for event-driven side effects and cross-domain communication. The anti-pattern is picking one protocol and using it everywhere — REST for everything creates cascading failure chains, Kafka for everything makes simple request-response flows unnecessarily complex.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Temporal coupling is the core risk** — synchronous chain A→B→C→D makes the slowest service determine everyone's latency.
- **Protobuf is 5–10× smaller than JSON** — bandwidth and parse-time savings compound at 10K+ internal RPC calls per second.
- **Kafka fan-out decouples producers from consumers** — one `OrderPlaced` event; adding a new consumer requires zero producer changes.
- **REST is the only option for external APIs** — browsers and partners can't install protobuf compilers; HTTP caching and curl work universally.
- **Production systems use all three** — REST at edge, gRPC for hot paths, Kafka for event-driven side effects.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
REST, gRPC, and Kafka are not interchangeable — each solves a different coupling problem, and the right choice depends on who is calling and whether the caller needs an immediate answer. Mature architectures use all three; using one protocol everywhere is the most common architectural mistake.

**REST — external facing:**
- The default for anything external-facing: browsers, mobile apps, and partners all speak HTTP and JSON natively
- Unmatched tooling — curl, Postman, Swagger, CDN caching; for internal calls under a few hundred RPS, REST is still fine because debugging simplicity outweighs the performance difference
- For internal calls, temporal coupling is the risk — a synchronous chain A→B→C→D makes the slowest service determine everyone's latency

**gRPC — internal hot paths:**
- Worth the switch when you have high-frequency internal calls — thousands per second — where Protobuf's binary encoding (5–10× smaller than JSON) and HTTP/2 multiplexing provide measurable latency improvement
- Strict schema contracts via `.proto` files catch breaking changes at compile time instead of at 2 AM when deserialization starts failing
- Cannot be used for browser clients or third-party partners without a grpc-web proxy

**Kafka — decoupled side effects:**
- The right choice when the producer doesn't need a response and multiple downstream services react to the same event — publish `OrderPlaced` once, and inventory, notifications, analytics, and fraud all process independently
- Breaks temporal coupling entirely — the producer returns immediately; consumers process at their own pace even after an outage and recovery

I recommend REST at the edge, gRPC for internal hot paths where performance is measured, and Kafka for cross-domain events where the producer doesn't need an immediate response.

sections.title: The Thread-Pool Drain That Takes Down Your Entire Fleet
sections.content:
Picture this: the inventory service starts responding in 8 seconds instead of 200ms. Without a circuit breaker, the order service keeps sending requests and each one occupies a thread for 8 seconds waiting for a response. At 50 requests per second, you have 400 threads blocked within a minute. The order service's thread pool is exhausted. Now it can't handle any requests — not even ones that don't touch inventory. Users see 503 errors on completely unrelated features. That's a **cascading failure**.

The circuit breaker pattern borrows from electrical engineering. When current exceeds a safe threshold, the breaker trips open and stops the flow — protecting the system from damage. In software, the "current" is the failure rate of a downstream dependency. When failures exceed a threshold, the breaker trips open and starts returning errors immediately (in microseconds, not seconds), giving the failing service time to recover while preventing the caller from drowning in blocked threads.

The pattern has three states that form a state machine. **CLOSED** is normal operation — all calls go through and the breaker records success/failure metrics. When the failure rate crosses a configured threshold (typically 50% over a sliding window), the breaker transitions to **OPEN** — all calls fail immediately without attempting the downstream call. After a configured wait duration (typically 10–30 seconds), the breaker moves to **HALF_OPEN** — a small number of probe calls are allowed through. If they succeed, the breaker returns to CLOSED. If they fail, it returns to OPEN.

The critical insight: a circuit breaker is **not** a retry mechanism. Retries amplify load on a struggling service. A circuit breaker does the opposite — it sheds load so the failing service can recover. In practice, you compose both: retry wraps the circuit breaker (outer), so the circuit breaker sees the aggregate result after retries, not each individual attempt.

Count-Based vs Time-Based Windows — And Why It Matters
Production Monitoring — Alert on Transitions, Not Failure Rates

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The circuit breaker pattern prevents cascading failures in synchronous microservice chains. When a downstream service degrades, the circuit breaker detects the pattern and starts failing fast — protecting the caller from exhausting its thread pool waiting for responses that won't arrive in time.

**How Resilience4j's three-state machine works:**
- CLOSED is normal — calls go through and failure metrics are recorded against a sliding window of the last N calls
- When failure rate exceeds the threshold (typically 50%), it transitions to OPEN — every call returns immediately with the fallback response, no downstream attempt is made
- After a wait duration (10–30 seconds), it moves to HALF_OPEN and lets a few probe calls through; success closes the breaker, failure reopens it

**Critical configuration decisions:**
- The `recordExceptions` filter is what most people miss — business validation errors like "invalid product ID" should NOT count as infrastructure failures and trip the breaker; only timeouts, connection refused, and 5xx should
- `slowCallDurationThreshold` catches degradation before hard failures appear — a service responding in 5 seconds ties up threads just as badly as a timeout; set it to 2–3× your expected p99 latency

**Composing with other patterns:**
- Always pair circuit breakers with bulkheads — separate thread pools per dependency so a failing inventory service can't exhaust the pool that payments and shipping also use
- Compose with retry as the outer decorator so the circuit breaker sees the aggregate outcome, not each individual retry attempt

I recommend alerting on state transitions (CLOSED→OPEN) rather than failure rates — a transition means users are getting degraded responses, which is a production incident.

sections.title: The Problem: One Request, Five Log Files, Zero Correlation
sections.content:
A user clicks "Place Order" and the request touches the API gateway, order service, inventory service, payment service, and notification service. The order fails. Where? You open five Kibana dashboards and search by timestamp, hoping the same second range catches the right log line in each service. It doesn't, because clocks are skewed by 200ms across hosts. You spend 40 minutes correlating logs that a trace ID would have linked in one click.

Distributed tracing solves this by assigning a single **trace ID** at the entry point (typically the API gateway) and propagating it in HTTP headers to every downstream call. Each service also generates a **span ID** for its portion of the work. Spans are linked into a tree that shows the full call path — which services were called, in what order, how long each took, and where the failure occurred.

The mental model is simple: a **trace** is the entire journey of one user request across all services. A **span** is one unit of work within that trace — a service processing the request, a database query, an HTTP call to a downstream dependency. Spans have parent-child relationships: the order service's span is the parent; the inventory and payment spans are children. The result is a flame graph showing exactly where time was spent and where errors occurred.

The standard propagation header is **W3C Trace Context** (`traceparent` / `tracestate`), which has replaced the older Zipkin B3 format. Using W3C headers ensures interoperability across languages, frameworks, and observability vendors — your Java services and your Go services and your Python scripts all participate in the same trace.

sections.title: Spring Boot 3 Auto-Instrumentation — Near-Zero Code Required
sections.content:
Spring Boot 3 integrated Micrometer Tracing as the native observability API, replacing the old Spring Cloud Sleuth library. The setup is two dependencies and three lines of YAML — most of the instrumentation happens automatically.

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
    <artifactId>micrometer-tracing-bridge-brave</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.zipkin.reporter2</groupId>
    <artifactId>zipkin-reporter-brave</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

```yaml
management:
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: 1.0         # 100% in dev; 0.05–0.10 in production
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service        # appears in trace metadata
logging:
  pattern:
    level: "%5p [${spring.application.name},%X{traceId},%X{spanId}]"
```

With this configuration, every log line automatically includes the trace and span IDs. When you search for `traceId=abc123` in your log aggregator, you get every log line from every service that participated in that request — in order.

The auto-instrumentation covers `RestTemplate`, `WebClient`, `RestClient`, Spring Data JPA, `@Async` methods, and scheduled tasks. Each outgoing HTTP call automatically injects the `traceparent` header; each incoming call extracts it. You don't write any propagation code. The only requirement is that you use Spring's HTTP clients instead of raw `java.net.HttpURLConnection` — Spring can only instrument what it controls.

sections.title: Custom Spans and Async Propagation — Where Auto-Instrumentation Falls Short
Sampling Strategy — The Cost vs Visibility Balance
sections.content:
Tracing 100% of requests in production is expensive. Each span generates metadata that must be collected, transmitted, stored, and indexed. At 10,000 RPS across 5 services with an average of 4 spans per request, that's 200,000 spans per second — roughly 50GB of storage per day in Zipkin or Jaeger.

The standard approach is **probability-based sampling** — trace a percentage of requests. Start at 5–10% for most services. This gives you enough traces for general latency analysis while keeping storage costs manageable. Keep the ability to **dynamically raise sampling** during incidents — a feature flag or config server change that bumps to 100% when you're actively debugging.

Even unsampled traces should have their IDs in log lines. The log pattern `%X{traceId}` works regardless of whether the trace is exported to Zipkin. This means you can always correlate logs by trace ID — you just won't have the visual flame graph in the trace UI. For the traces that are sampled, set a retention policy (7–14 days) to prevent storage from growing indefinitely.

Sampling can be smarter than random. **Error-biased sampling** always exports traces that contain an error span, regardless of the probability setting. This ensures you always have trace data for failures, which are the traces you actually need during incidents. Resilience4j and Micrometer support this through custom `Sampler` implementations that check the span's error state before deciding whether to export.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Trace = full journey, span = one unit of work** — trace ID ties all services together; parent-child relationships build a flame graph.
- **W3C `traceparent` header** — the interoperability standard; ensures Java, Go, Python, and Node services contribute to the same trace.
- **100% sampling melts storage** — 10K RPS × 5 services × 4 spans ≈ 50GB/day; use 5–10% with error-biased override.
- **Async boundaries silently break traces** — Kafka consumers and `@Async` lose context unless you inject/extract headers at boundaries.
- **Log correlation works without sampling** — `%X{traceId}` in log pattern adds trace IDs even for unsampled traces.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Distributed tracing solves the problem of debugging requests that span multiple services. When an order fails in production, you need to know exactly where it failed — the gateway, the order service, the inventory check, or the payment call. Without tracing, you're correlating five log files by timestamp and hoping server clocks are synchronized.

**How it works:**
- A trace ID is assigned at the entry point and propagated in W3C `traceparent` headers to every downstream call; each service generates a span ID for its work, with parent-child relationships building a flame graph
- In Spring Boot 3, Micrometer Tracing handles propagation automatically through `RestTemplate`, `WebClient`, and Spring Data without code changes; add the log pattern `%X{traceId}` to correlate logs across services with a single search

**The async boundary gotcha:**
- When the order service publishes to Kafka, the consumer loses trace context because there's no HTTP header to extract from the message
- You must explicitly inject the trace context into Kafka record headers at publish time, and extract it in the consumer; without this, the consumer's trace appears orphaned with no connection to the originating request

**Sampling strategy:**
- Never sample at 100% — at 10K RPS across 5 services, that's 50GB of trace data per day in Zipkin or Jaeger
- Use 5–10% probability sampling with error-biased override so failures are always captured regardless of the sampling rate; log correlation with `%X{traceId}` still works on unsampled requests

I recommend wiring Micrometer Tracing from day one — retrofitting trace propagation through async boundaries is significantly harder than getting it right at service creation time.

sections.title: Why `@Transactional` Stops Working Across Service Boundaries
sections.content:
In a monolith, placing an order is one database transaction: insert the order, reserve inventory, charge payment, schedule shipping. If payment fails, everything rolls back automatically. `@Transactional` handles it because all four operations hit the same database.

With microservices, each service owns its own database. The order service has its database. Inventory has its own. Payments has its own. There's no shared transaction coordinator that can atomically commit across three separate PostgreSQL instances. You might think **two-phase commit (2PC)** solves this — a coordinator tells all participants to prepare, then commit. In theory, yes. In practice, 2PC has two fatal problems at scale: if the coordinator crashes between the prepare and commit phases, all participants are **blocked** holding locks until the coordinator recovers (minutes to hours), and the network round-trips required for the two phases add latency that compounds with every participant.

The Saga pattern takes a fundamentally different approach. Instead of one atomic transaction, it breaks the operation into a **sequence of local transactions**, each within a single service's database. Each local transaction publishes an event or sends a command to trigger the next step. If a step fails, the saga executes **compensating transactions** to undo the previous steps — not a database rollback, but explicit business logic that reverses the effect.

The mental shift is accepting that between steps, the system is in an **inconsistent state**. The order exists but payment hasn't been charged. Inventory is reserved but shipping hasn't been scheduled. The saga guarantees that the system will eventually reach a consistent state — either all steps succeed or all are compensated. This is **eventual consistency**, and your UI must be designed to show intermediate states ("Processing your order...") rather than a definitive success until the saga completes.

sections.title: Choreography — Events Without a Central Brain
Orchestration — A Central Coordinator That Knows the Whole Story
Compensating Transactions — The Hard Part Nobody Talks About
Key Points
sections.content:
- **2PC blocks on coordinator failure** — if coordinator crashes between prepare and commit, all participants hold locks indefinitely.
- **Choreography: no coordinator, no visibility** — each service reacts to events; past 5 services the workflow becomes hard to trace.
- **Orchestration: visible workflow, single dependency** — the coordinator shows the full state machine but must be persistent and highly available.
- **Compensation ≠ rollback** — reversing a credit card charge is a refund API call, not a database rollback; must be idempotent.
- **Stuck sagas signal dead-letter problems** — alert when a saga stays in intermediate state beyond SLA; usually a message in a DLQ.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Distributed transactions are one of the hardest problems in microservices because `@Transactional` cannot span multiple databases. Two-phase commit technically works but holds locks across all participants until every database votes — unacceptable at scale. The Saga pattern replaces one atomic transaction with a sequence of local transactions, each within a single service's database.

**Compensating transactions — the key insight:**
- Compensation is not a database rollback — when payment succeeded but inventory is out of stock, you issue a refund, which is a new forward operation creating a credit record
- Compensating transactions must be idempotent because at-least-once delivery can trigger them multiple times — a compensation command arriving twice must produce the same outcome as once
- Every step in a saga must have a defined compensation that can be executed independently

**Choreography vs orchestration:**
- Choreography has no central coordinator — each service reacts to others' events; clean for 2–3 step flows but becomes unmanageable past 5 services where the interaction graph is invisible
- Orchestration uses a dedicated state machine that sends commands, tracks which steps completed, and drives compensation when something fails — the workflow is in one class, easy to debug and test, but the coordinator needs to be highly available and persistent

**Operational visibility:**
- Monitor saga duration and alert when one stays in an intermediate state longer than your SLA (1–5 minutes for order flows) — the most common cause is a consumer crash with an unprocessed message in a dead-letter queue

I recommend orchestration for business-critical sagas with conditional logic or many participants, and choreography only for simple linear flows with 2–3 services.

sections.title: Why a Shared Database Turns Microservices Back Into a Monolith
sections.content:
The most common way teams accidentally rebuild a monolith is by sharing a database. The order service and the inventory service both connect to the same PostgreSQL instance. The order service runs `SELECT p.name FROM inventory.products p JOIN orders o ON ...` — a direct cross-schema join. It works, it's fast, and it's a trap.

The moment the inventory team needs to rename `products.name` to `products.display_name`, they can't — the order service's query will break. They have to coordinate the migration across both teams. Schema changes require synchronized deployments. The inventory team can't switch to MongoDB for catalog search without rewriting the order service. The services are independently deployable in theory but coupled at the data layer in practice.

**Database-per-service** means each service is the exclusive owner of its tables. No other service reads or writes them directly. Cross-service data access happens through APIs (REST/gRPC) or events (Kafka). This gives each team full control over their schema, storage technology, and migration schedule.

The common misconception is that "database per service" means separate physical database instances from day one. It doesn't have to. **Separate schemas within the same PostgreSQL cluster** work fine as a starting point — as long as you enforce access control. Each service gets its own database user that can only access its own schema. Network policies block direct cross-service database connections. The key is the ownership boundary, not the physical infrastructure.

sections.title: Cross-Service Data Access — Three Patterns, Three Trade-offs
The Outbox Pattern — Atomic State + Event Publishing
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Separate schemas, strict grants** — database-per-service doesn't require separate clusters on day one; schema-level isolation enforces the boundary.
- **Cross-schema JOINs recreate monolith coupling** — order-service querying `inventory.products` means schema changes require coordinated deployments.
- **API calls for fresh writes, events for read replicas** — synchronous for consistency-critical writes.
- **Outbox pattern eliminates dual-write risk** — write business data and event in the same transaction; relay to Kafka via polling or Debezium.
- **Foreign keys can't span databases** — store referenced entity's ID and validate via API or event sync; handle deletions via domain events.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Each microservice should own its database exclusively. The moment two services share a database, schema changes require coordination, storage technology choices are coupled, and you've recreated the monolith at the data layer. In practice, separate schemas with strict access grants enforce the boundary without requiring separate database instances on day one.

**Cross-service data access patterns:**
- Synchronous API call — gives you fresh data but creates a runtime dependency; if inventory is down, the order service can't display product names
- Event-driven denormalization — the order service maintains a local read replica updated by consuming inventory events; fast and resilient, but data can lag by 100ms to a few seconds
- Choose by consistency requirement: synchronous for writes and low-volume fresh reads, event-driven for high-traffic read paths where slight staleness is acceptable

**The dual-write problem:**
- Saving to the database and then publishing to Kafka creates a crash window — if the application crashes between those two operations, the event is lost forever
- The Outbox pattern solves this: write the event to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the business entity; a separate process relays outbox rows to Kafka
- Polling is simpler (a `@Scheduled` method); Debezium WAL tailing delivers in under 100ms but requires a Kafka Connect cluster

I recommend the Outbox pattern at every point where state changes need reliable event publishing — it's the only way to guarantee atomicity between the database write and the event.

sections.title: The Problem: 20 Services, 5 Languages, One Security Policy
sections.content:
Cross-cutting concerns in microservices — mutual TLS, circuit breaking, retry policies, distributed tracing, rate limiting — need to be consistent across every service. The library approach means every team implements these using language-specific libraries: Resilience4j for Java, Polly for C#, a custom Go middleware, a Python decorator. You end up with 5 implementations of the same circuit breaker policy, each configured slightly differently, each with its own bugs.

The sidecar pattern extracts these concerns from the application entirely. A lightweight proxy — typically **Envoy** — runs as a separate container in the same Kubernetes pod as your application. Every inbound and outbound network request passes through the proxy transparently. The application code makes a plain HTTP call to `http://inventory-service:8080/api/stock` — it doesn't know that the sidecar is intercepting the call to apply mTLS encryption, retry policies, circuit breaking, and trace header injection.

A **service mesh** is what you get when you deploy sidecars to every service and manage them centrally. **Istio** is the most widely adopted mesh. It has two planes: the **data plane** is the fleet of Envoy sidecars handling actual traffic. The **control plane** (Istiod) pushes configuration and certificates to all sidecars, so policy changes propagate across the fleet without redeploying any application. You declare "all services use mTLS" in one YAML file, and Istiod configures every sidecar to enforce it.

The honest trade-off: each Envoy sidecar adds **1–5ms latency per hop** and consumes **50–100MB memory** per pod. For a 200-pod deployment, that's 10–20GB of memory just for sidecars. The mesh also introduces a new failure domain — sidecar crashes, certificate rotation failures, control plane outages — that your team must learn to operate.

sections.title: The Data Plane — Envoy Sidecars Doing the Real Work
sections.content:
Envoy is a high-performance C++ proxy originally built at Lyft. In the sidecar deployment model, it intercepts all traffic entering and leaving the application container via iptables rules that redirect network traffic through the proxy.

The interception is transparent to the application. When your Spring Boot service calls `http://inventory-service:8080`, the request is intercepted by the local Envoy, which applies the configured policies: encrypt with mTLS, add trace headers, apply retry policy (3 retries with exponential backoff), enforce a 5-second timeout, and route to a healthy instance of inventory-service using round-robin load balancing. If the circuit breaker for inventory is open, Envoy returns a 503 without sending the request upstream.

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: inventory-service
spec:
  host: inventory-service
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      http:
        h2UpgradePolicy: UPGRADE    # use HTTP/2 between sidecars
        maxRequestsPerConnection: 100
    outlierDetection:
      consecutive5xxErrors: 3       # eject instance after 3 consecutive 5xx
      interval: 10s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
```

The `outlierDetection` configuration is Envoy's circuit breaker — it ejects unhealthy instances from the load balancing pool rather than stopping all traffic. This is more granular than application-level circuit breakers: instead of blocking all calls to inventory-service, it only removes the specific instance that's failing. If you have 5 inventory pods and one is unhealthy, the sidecar routes around it while the other 4 continue serving.

sections.title: The Control Plane — Istiod as the Central Brain
sections.content:
Istiod is a single binary that provides three functions: **Pilot** (traffic management — pushes routing rules and load balancing config to sidecars), **Citadel** (security — provisions and rotates mTLS certificates for every sidecar), and **Galley** (configuration — validates and distributes Istio CRDs).

When you apply a VirtualService resource in Kubernetes, Istiod translates it into Envoy configuration and pushes it to every relevant sidecar via xDS (Envoy's discovery service protocol). The sidecars apply the new configuration without restarting — traffic shifts happen in seconds with zero downtime.

mTLS is the mesh's most valuable security feature. Without a mesh, implementing mutual TLS between 50 services means each team must manage certificates, configure trust stores, and handle rotation. With Istio, mTLS is a one-line policy change.

```yaml
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: production
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT    # all pod-to-pod traffic is encrypted and authenticated
```

Citadel provisions a unique SPIFFE identity certificate to each service, rotates them automatically (default: every 24 hours), and the sidecars handle the TLS handshake transparently. The application never sees the certificates — it still makes plain HTTP calls, and the sidecar encrypts the traffic.

The control plane itself must be highly available. If Istiod goes down, existing sidecar configurations continue working (the data plane is decoupled), but new configuration changes won't propagate and certificate rotations will stall. Run Istiod with at least 2 replicas and monitor certificate expiration.

sections.title: When the Mesh Isn't Worth It — And What to Use Instead
sections.content:
The service mesh is not free. Beyond the latency and memory overhead, it introduces operational complexity that requires a dedicated platform team. Certificate rotation failures, sidecar injection bugs during rolling deployments, Envoy version upgrades, control plane high availability — these become your team's responsibilities.

For teams running **fewer than 15–20 services**, the library approach is usually sufficient and simpler. Resilience4j handles circuit breaking. Spring Security handles mTLS (or skip it with network-level isolation in a VPC). Micrometer Tracing handles distributed tracing. Each library is configured per-service, but with shared Spring Boot starter dependencies, the configuration is consistent enough.

The **mesh becomes worth it** when: you have a polyglot fleet (Java + Go + Python + Node) where per-language libraries don't exist or diverge in behavior, you need zero-trust networking with enforced mTLS across all services (compliance requirements like PCI-DSS or SOC2), you want advanced traffic management (canary deployments routing 5% to the new version, traffic mirroring for shadow testing), or you have a platform team that can operate the mesh as an internal product.

If you're adopting Istio, do it incrementally. Start with observability-only mode (telemetry, no policy enforcement), then add permissive mTLS, then strict mTLS, and finally traffic management rules. Each phase should run for at least 2 weeks in production before advancing. Benchmark p99 latency at each phase to quantify the overhead — if the added latency is unacceptable for your SLOs, you need to tune Envoy's resource limits or reconsider the mesh for that particular service path.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Transparent interception** — Envoy sidecars redirect all pod traffic via iptables; application makes plain HTTP calls, unaware of mTLS or tracing.
- **Control plane vs data plane** — Istiod pushes config and certificates to sidecars.
- **Per-instance circuit breaking** — Envoy's `outlierDetection` ejects unhealthy instances from the pool instead of blocking all traffic.
- **1–5ms latency + 50–100MB memory per sidecar** — at 200 pods, that's 10–20GB of memory for sidecars alone.
- **Library-first for <20 services** — Resilience4j + Spring Security + Micrometer covers most needs without mesh complexity.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The sidecar pattern deploys a proxy — typically Envoy — alongside each service container. All network traffic passes through the proxy transparently, so cross-cutting concerns like mTLS, circuit breaking, retries, and distributed tracing are handled without touching application code. The application makes a plain HTTP call; the sidecar handles the rest.

**How a service mesh works:**
- A service mesh is what emerges when you deploy sidecars to every service and manage them centrally; Istio has two planes — the data plane is the Envoy fleet handling traffic, and the control plane (Istiod) pushes configuration and certificates
- One YAML change — `mtls.mode: STRICT` — encrypts every service-to-service call without any code changes; per-instance circuit breaking via `outlierDetection` ejects unhealthy pods instead of blocking all traffic
- If Istiod goes down, existing config keeps working but updates stall — the data plane is resilient to control plane failures

**The real cost:**
- Each sidecar adds 1–5ms latency per hop and 50–100MB memory; at 200 pods, sidecars alone consume 10–20GB and you need a team that can operate the mesh
- Debug sidecar injection, handle certificate rotation, manage control plane availability — this is non-trivial operational overhead for teams without mesh experience

**When the mesh pays off:**
- Polyglot fleets where library-based solutions would require separate implementations per language
- Compliance-driven mTLS requirements where the alternative is per-service certificate management
- Advanced traffic management like canary routing, traffic mirroring, or fault injection testing

I recommend library-first (Resilience4j + Micrometer + Spring Security) for fewer than 20 services in a single language; the mesh becomes worth it at scale with polyglot or compliance requirements.

sections.title: Why Big-Bang Rewrites Fail — And What Works Instead
sections.content:
The instinct when facing a messy monolith is to rewrite it from scratch. Build the new microservices in parallel, feature-freeze the monolith, and switch over on launch day. This approach has a documented failure rate above **70%** for production systems. The most famous example is Netscape 6 — a complete rewrite that took three years, during which the old product couldn't be improved and competitors ate market share.

The Strangler Fig pattern, named by Martin Fowler after a tropical vine that grows around a tree and eventually replaces it, takes the opposite approach. The monolith **keeps running**. You place an API gateway in front of it. New functionality is built as microservices. Existing functionality is extracted one module at a time. At each step, the gateway routes specific paths to the new service while everything else still goes to the monolith. Users never notice the transition.

The reason this works where rewrites fail: there's **no feature-freeze**. The monolith continues serving production traffic and receiving bug fixes throughout the migration. Each extracted service is validated independently — if the user service extraction goes badly, you revert one routing rule at the gateway and users are back on the monolith's user module within seconds. The blast radius of a failure is one service, not the entire system.

The prerequisite is a **well-understood domain**. If you don't know where the boundaries are, you'll extract the wrong modules and end up with services that constantly call each other — a distributed monolith. Spend 2–3 months identifying bounded contexts through Domain-Driven Design workshops before cutting any code. The quality of the migration depends entirely on the quality of the boundary identification.

sections.title: Phase 1 — Gateway Routing and the First Extraction
sections.content:
The first step is placing a reverse proxy or API gateway in front of the monolith. Initially, it passes everything through. This non-functional change establishes the routing layer you'll use for the entire migration.

```yaml
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: monolith-catchall
          uri: http://monolith:8080
          predicates:
            - Path=/**          # everything goes to monolith initially
```

For the first extraction, pick a module that is **well-bounded, low-risk, and read-heavy**. User profile management and notification preferences are common first candidates — they have clear boundaries, don't touch revenue flows, and are mostly reads. Payments, checkout, and order management come later when the team has migration experience.

Extract the module into a new service with its own database, API, and CI/CD pipeline. Then update the gateway to route the relevant paths.

```yaml
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: user-service
          uri: lb://USER-SERVICE
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/users/**    # extracted paths go to new service
          order: 1                  # higher priority than catchall
        - id: monolith-catchall
          uri: http://monolith:8080
          predicates:
            - Path=/**              # everything else still goes to monolith
          order: 100
```

The `order` field matters — routes are evaluated in priority order, so the specific service route must take precedence over the monolith catchall. Without explicit ordering, a request to `/api/users/123` might still reach the monolith.

sections.title: The Anti-Corruption Layer — Translating Between Old and New Worlds
Database Strangling — The Part That's Harder Than the Code
sections.content:
Extracting HTTP routes is the easy part. The hard part is **migrating data ownership**. If the new user service still reads from the monolith's `USERS` table, it can't be independently deployed, scaled, or migrated to a different database. You've moved code but not ownership.

The database migration runs in parallel with code extraction. Set up **Change Data Capture** (Debezium) to replicate the monolith's user tables to the new service's database in near-real-time. The new service reads from its own database. Compare results against the monolith using shadow traffic to verify data consistency.

Once reads are verified consistent (run a reconciliation job for at least a week), switch writes. The new service becomes the authoritative writer. Debezium direction reverses — the new service publishes change events that the monolith consumes to keep its local copy in sync during the transition. After all monolith code that referenced user data is removed, drop the monolith's user tables.

The shadow testing phase is critical. Run both code paths simultaneously and compare outputs. Log discrepancies without affecting user-facing responses. This surfaces edge cases that unit tests miss — timezone handling differences, null vs empty string semantics, character encoding issues, pagination ordering differences.

Maintain a **rollback path** at every step. The gateway routing change is a one-line YAML update to revert traffic to the monolith. Keep the monolith's code for the extracted module intact but inactive for at least one full release cycle after cutover. Document the rollback procedure in a runbook and rehearse it during off-peak hours.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Big-bang rewrite failure rate >70%** — second system must achieve full feature parity before anyone benefits.
- **Gateway routing = the migration lever** — one YAML change redirects traffic from monolith to new service; rollback is seconds.
- **First extraction: low-risk, read-heavy** — user profiles and notifications before payments and checkout.
- **Anti-corruption layer prevents legacy leakage** — translate `USR_ADDR_LN1` to `address.line1` at the boundary without inheriting 2008 naming.
- **Database strangling via CDC** — Debezium replicates monolith tables; shadow-test for ≥1 week before switching writes.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The Strangler Fig pattern is the opposite of a big-bang rewrite. You place an API gateway in front of the existing monolith, extract one module at a time into a new service, and route traffic to it at the gateway — the monolith keeps running throughout with no feature freeze, no launch day, and no all-or-nothing risk.

**The migration sequence:**
- Start with a low-risk, well-bounded module — user profiles or notifications, not payments; build the new service with its own database and API, then update the gateway to route the relevant path to the new service
- If something breaks, one routing change sends traffic back to the monolith — rollback is seconds, not a deployment cycle
- The monolith's code stays intact for at least one release cycle after cutover, so regression is always available

**Database migration — the underestimated part:**
- Redirecting HTTP routes to a new service that still reads from the monolith's database creates a distributed monolith — the service is independent in name only
- Replicate data via CDC (Debezium), shadow-test reads for at least a week, then switch writes; the new service becomes the authoritative data owner
- The anti-corruption layer translates between the monolith's legacy data model and the new service's clean domain model — without it, you inherit 15-year-old column names and business rules baked into database schema

**The test of real independence:**
- If you can't deploy the extracted service without coordinating with another team or service, you have a distributed monolith, not microservices

I recommend Strangler Fig as the only safe migration approach — big-bang rewrites fail more than 70% of the time because the second system must achieve full feature parity before delivering any value.
